# 1. Executive Summary

This document sets out a plan to take the End-to-End Microservices Integration Testing SaaS platform from concept to a first releasable product. The companion architecture and specification documents describe what the full platform should eventually become; this plan answers a narrower and more urgent question: what is the smallest version that delivers real value to a real user, and how is it built without overcommitting?

A note on naming. The platform's working title carries the word “SaaS” because that is the eventual delivery model the cloud and enterprise tiers are designed around. The MVP itself is deliberately not a SaaS — it is a free local tool with no backend, no subscription, and no hosted state — because the central hypothesis must be tested before any cloud infrastructure is built. The name describes the destination, not the first stop.

The plan is built around a single discipline. The full vision is large — it spans a cloud execution fabric, autonomous agents, a performance-testing lab, and enterprise identity integration. Attempting all of it before shipping anything would expose the project to years of risk before a single user could validate the central premise. The Minimum Viable Product therefore deliberately defers the cloud, the agents, the lab, and enterprise SSO, and concentrates the entire first effort on proving the one hypothesis everything else depends on: **that a declarative YAML language, compiled to C# and orchestrated by .NET Aspire, makes integration testing meaningfully easier for .NET teams.**

Concretely, the MVP is a locally executing testing tool. A developer installs it, writes tests in the YAML DSL with full VSCode support, and runs them against a microservice topology that the tool provisions on their own machine. There is no cloud backend, no subscription, and no agentic automation. The plan estimates this scope at roughly twenty-four weeks for a small dedicated team, organised into five phases, and it identifies the principal risks and the decision point at which the project commits to building the cloud tier.

## 1.1 The MVP hypothesis

> **Hypothesis under test**
>
> If we give .NET teams a declarative YAML language that compiles to Roslyn C# and orchestrates their real dependencies through .NET Aspire, they will find integration testing enough easier that they adopt the tool, author non-trivial suites, and ask for cloud execution. The MVP exists to confirm or refute this before any cloud infrastructure is built.

Every scoping decision in this plan traces back to that hypothesis. A feature is in the MVP if it is necessary to test the hypothesis, and out of it otherwise. This is what justifies deferring genuinely valuable capabilities such as the cloud fabric: they are not needed to learn whether the core idea works, and building them first would mean spending the largest costs before earning the most important evidence.

## 1.2 A note on the vendor entity

Customers will ask, from the first conversation, who they are taking software from. The plan therefore names this explicitly: a single corporate entity is incorporated in Phase 3 to be the vendor of record for the platform, with the product's name (also chosen in Phase 3) as its trading identity. The entity carries the trademark, signs DPAs and software licences for enterprise pilots, owns the open-source repositories, and is the party named in procurement and third-party-software-request paperwork. Even the free Indie tier requires this, because enterprise procurement teams need to record the rights-holder of any software in use, free or paid. The Czech Republic / EU jurisdiction is the working assumption based on the team's location; this is revisited in Phase 3 with legal advice before incorporation.

# 2. Users, Market, and Positioning

Before scope, before timeline, before risk, a product needs to know who it is for. This section names the people the MVP is designed for, the alternatives those people use today, and the position the platform takes against them. A plan without this section can produce a technically excellent tool that nobody specifically wants; the rest of this document depends on the answers below being correct, so they are stated explicitly rather than assumed.

## 2.1 Primary persona — the platform engineer at a microservices-heavy .NET shop

The primary user is a senior backend or platform engineer at a mid-sized to large .NET-stack organisation — typically a financial-services, e-commerce, or B2B SaaS business with thirty or more microservices in production, owned across half a dozen teams. They write C# daily, are comfortable with Docker and Kubernetes, and have between five and twenty years of professional experience. They sit somewhere on the spectrum between senior engineer and tech lead, and they care about the health of the integration boundary because they are the person paged when it breaks.

Their day is shaped by a recurring frustration: the team's unit tests are green, the team's contract tests pass, but the system in staging still breaks in ways that only appear when the real Kafka, the real Postgres, and the real downstream service are wired together. Their current tools force a choice between hand-rolled xUnit suites with WebApplicationFactory (which work but ossify and become a maintenance burden), Postman collections (which the QA team owns and the engineers never trust), or expensive Kubernetes-in-a-laptop setups that take fifteen minutes to come up. The cost they actually feel is not test authoring — it is the loop of “write test, wait three minutes for the environment, find out the test was wrong, repeat.” They would adopt a tool that compresses that loop dramatically, runs against real dependencies, and produces reports they can trust without spelunking through container logs.

## 2.2 Secondary persona — the staff or principal engineer setting platform-wide patterns

The secondary user is the staff or principal engineer who chooses the testing strategy for the whole organisation. They do not personally write every test, but they decide what the rest of the engineering team standardises on, and they own the relationship with the platform's sponsor in finance or engineering leadership. Their job-to-be-done is not “write a test” — it is “make integration testing a sustainably good experience across forty engineers,” which is a different and harder problem. They evaluate tools against the criteria of long-term maintainability, community health, security posture, and total cost of ownership rather than first-impression authoring speed. They are the budget owner for the eventual cloud tier.

## 2.3 Non-users — segments the MVP is not designed for

Naming who the MVP is not for is as important as naming who it is for, because a plan that tries to serve every segment serves none well. The MVP is explicitly not built for: front-end-heavy teams whose integration concerns are browser and CDN behaviour (Playwright, Cypress, and similar serve them well); teams on the JVM, Python, or Node stacks (the platform's value depends on first-class C# integration); QA-led organisations where test authoring is centralised away from the engineers who write the code (the platform is built around author-developer parity); and very small teams of fewer than five engineers running a handful of services (the orchestration machinery is over-investment at that scale). These segments may become addressable later; they are not the wedge.

## 2.4 The market the platform competes in

Pilot teams will not adopt the platform in a vacuum. They have testing tools they use today, and the plan owes them — and itself — an honest account of how the platform sits against those tools. The table below names five categories of alternative the platform must answer for; the next subsection states the platform's distinguishing claim.

| Alternative | What it does well | Where the platform is meant to do better |
|---|---|---|
| xUnit / NUnit + WebApplicationFactory + Testcontainers (hand-rolled) | Mature, free, runs on any CI, gives full control. The status-quo choice in many .NET shops. | Hand-rolled suites accrete framework code that drifts; orchestration is reinvented per project; reporting is xUnit's, which has no native concept of asynchronous propagation. The platform replaces the framework, leaving the team to write only the tests. |
| Postman / Newman collections | Excellent for synchronous REST testing; familiar to QA and engineers alike. | Cannot reach a Kafka topic, a database row, or an outbound webhook; collection files become unmaintainable beyond a few dozen requests; orchestration is out of scope and left to the user. |
| k6 / Gatling / JMeter | Strong at load and performance; some support for assertions. | Built for load testing, not functional integration; multi-step transactions across asynchronous channels are not a first-class concept; reports are time-series, not verdict-with-evidence. |
| SpecFlow / Reqnroll (BDD on .NET) | Readable Gherkin scenarios; familiar to product stakeholders; mature .NET tooling. | Step bindings reintroduce the imperative-test maintenance burden the platform exists to remove; orchestration of real dependencies is out of scope; no native asynchrony model. |
| Bespoke Kubernetes-based test environments | Realistic at scale; allows multi-team integration. | Startup is slow (often minutes), per-developer cost is high, and the path from a failing test to a debuggable local environment is long. The platform's local-Aspire choice is faster and cheaper for the same coverage. |

*Table 2.1 — The competitive landscape the MVP must position against. Each row is a category, not a single product, and the right-hand column is the platform's working claim rather than a marketing slogan.*

## 2.5 The platform's positioning claim

> **Positioning, in one sentence**
>
> For senior .NET engineers responsible for the integration health of a microservices estate, the platform is the only declarative testing tool that runs scenarios end-to-end across real REST, Kafka, database, and webhook dependencies — with reports that explain asynchronous failures rather than reducing them to timeouts — in the developer's own loop, on their own machine, in seconds rather than minutes.

Two parts of this claim are deliberate and defensible against the alternatives in §2.4. The first is “declarative … end-to-end across real dependencies” — every alternative either gives up on real dependencies (Postman), gives up on multi-step transactions (k6), or gives up on the declarative form (hand-rolled xUnit). The second is “reports that explain asynchronous failures rather than reducing them to timeouts” — this is the reporting layer's polling timeline, captured-variable thread, and structured event stream, and it is the feature most directly visible against the alternatives. The plan's success criteria in section 4.2 are explicitly tied to this claim: if pilot teams do not experience these two advantages, the claim is wrong and the plan should be revisited.

## 2.6 A note on the product name

The working title used throughout these documents — “End-to-End Microservices Integration Testing SaaS” — is a descriptor, not a product name. A real product name is needed before launch, because launching under the working title commits the project to a name nobody chose and that is hard to escape later. The plan treats naming as a Phase 3 deliverable so that the documentation set, the GitHub organisation, the docs URL, and the launch artifacts in Phase 4 can all be produced under the chosen name rather than under the working title.

# 3. MVP Scope Definition

Scope is the most important section of this plan, because an MVP succeeds or fails on the discipline of its boundary. This section states explicitly what the first release contains and, with equal precision, what it does not.

## 3.1 In scope

The MVP delivers a coherent, genuinely useful local testing tool. The capabilities below are mutually reinforcing — each is necessary for the others to be worth having.

| Capability | What the MVP includes |
|---|---|
| **The YAML DSL (core)** | The four top-level sections and the six step families — http, mq-publish, mq-expect, db-assert, webhook-listen, and script — sufficient to express the reference scenario end to end. |
| **Core provider set** | Six Core providers shipping with the engine under Apache 2.0: http.rest, mq-publish.kafka, mq-expect.kafka, db-assert.postgres, webhook-listen.http, and script.csharp. Together they execute the reference scenario unchanged. |
| **Provider SDK and registry** | The source-level contract (IStepProvider, IStepBinder, IStepValidator, IStepCompiler, IResourceContributor), the reflection-based StepKindRegistry, the JSON Schema composition mechanism, and the CONTRIBUTING.md that opens community contribution from day one. |
| **YAML-to-CSX compiler** | Parsing to an AST, JSON Schema validation, CSX generation, and Roslyn compilation using the compile-once, collectible-load-context pattern that prevents memory leaks. |
| **Aspire orchestration** | Programmatic AppHost construction, health-gated startup, service discovery, build-once-per-suite fixtures, and Respawn-based state reset — for local Docker only. |
| **Test data seeding** | A declarative environment.seed block applying reference SQL files, document fixtures, and broker warm-up messages after the topology is healthy and before the first step; the script step as the factory escape hatch for data created through the system's own APIs. |
| **Secrets management** | The ${secret:…} reference syntax with environment-variable and HashiCorp Vault sources, runtime resolution, and report-layer redaction so credentials never enter source control, logs, or reports. |
| **Test runner (selection and parallelism)** | Beyond the headless CLI: a composable selection language over tag, ownership, path, and change-set; scenario-level parallelism bounded by a concurrency budget; the per-scenario isolation contract; watch mode for local iteration. |
| **Verification modes** | IMMEDIATE and RETRY, with RETRY compiling to bounded exponential-backoff polling via Polly. |
| **Variable capture** | JSONPath and XPath extraction into the shared context, and brace-syntax substitution across steps. |
| **VSCode extension (core)** | Schema-driven YAML autocomplete and validation, and embedded C# IntelliSense in script steps via the .NET language server. |
| **Test runner CLI** | A headless command-line runner with deterministic exit codes, suitable for invocation from a CI pipeline. |
| **Local result reporting** | Per-step outcomes using the verdict taxonomy — pass, fail, environment error — surfaced in the CLI and the editor. |
| **Reporting surface (five-layer)** | The structured JSON-Lines event stream the engine emits, the rich terminal renderer with the polling timeline and the captured-variable thread, the standalone HTML report written to disk, JUnit XML for CI gates, and the VSCode Test Explorer integration. Together these turn the platform's investment in asynchronous-first design into a developer-facing story rather than a forensic exercise. |

*Table 3.1 — Capabilities included in the MVP.*

## 3.2 Out of scope

The capabilities below are part of the full vision and are deliberately excluded from the MVP. For each, the table records why it is deferred — in every case the reason is that it is not required to test the core hypothesis and that building it early would front-load cost and risk.

| Deferred capability | Why it is out of scope for the MVP |
|---|---|
| **Testcontainer Cloud fabric** | Remote Docker proxying, SSH tunnelling, reverse port forwarding, and Ryuk in the cloud are the single largest engineering investment. They are only worth building once local adoption confirms demand. |
| **Agentic automation** | The Planner, Generator, and Healer agents add value on top of a working DSL; they cannot be evaluated until the DSL itself is proven and in real use. |
| **Performance Testing LAB** | Containerised load injection and Virtual-User-Hour metering depend on the cloud fabric and on a billing system, neither of which exists in the MVP. |
| **Enterprise tier and SSO** | SAML / OIDC integration, RBAC, on-premises Helm packaging, and audit logging serve a customer segment the MVP is not yet trying to reach. |
| **Billing and subscriptions** | The MVP is a free local tool; there is no paid tier to bill, so no billing system is built. |
| **The Wave-2 provider catalogue** | Providers beyond the Core six — db-assert.sqlserver, db-assert.oracle, db-assert.mongodb, db-assert.elasticsearch, db-assert.redis, mq-publish.rabbitmq, mq-publish.servicebus, mq-publish.sqs, rpc.grpc, http.soap, and the long tail — are out of MVP scope as deliverables, but the Provider SDK in scope above is the pathway by which they arrive: each is a community pull request rather than an engine change, and the architecture is deliberately designed so that the first Verified-tier providers can begin landing the day after v1.0 ships. |
| **Conditional and parallel steps** | The DSL models a single linear sequence in the MVP; richer control flow is a deliberate post-MVP language decision. |
| **Advanced data and secret sources** | Anonymised production-data snapshot pipelines and cloud secret managers (Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) are designed for but not built in the MVP; the seed block and the ${secret:…} syntax are forward-compatible with them, so they are configuration additions rather than redesigns. |
| **Mid-suite failure recovery** | If the engine crashes partway through a long suite, the MVP re-runs the suite from the start rather than resuming. Checkpoint-and-resume is a post-MVP optimisation; the stance is stated so its absence is a known choice, not a surprise. |
| **Automated migration tooling** | No tool converts existing Postman, k6, xUnit, or SpecFlow tests automatically. Worked porting examples are authored during the pilot (section 8.5) so teams have a clear manual path; an automated converter is explicitly out of scope. |

*Table 3.2 — Capabilities deferred beyond the MVP, with rationale.*

## 3.3 The scope boundary as a principle

The two tables above share one logic. Everything in scope is required to let a developer experience the core promise — write a declarative test, run it against real dependencies, get a trustworthy result — entirely on their own machine. Everything out of scope is either an enhancement of that experience or a different customer segment. The boundary is drawn at the local topology precisely because the local topology is the only one that needs no backend, no accounts, and no infrastructure spend, which makes it the fastest and cheapest way to put the hypothesis in front of real users.

# 4. Objectives and Success Criteria

An MVP needs measurable success criteria, because its purpose is to produce evidence, and evidence requires something to measure. This section states what the MVP must achieve and how the team will know whether it has.

## 4.1 Primary objectives

1. **Prove the authoring experience. **A developer unfamiliar with the tool can write the reference scenario — a four-technology transaction — as a YAML file, with editor support, in under an hour.
1. **Prove orchestration reliability. **The same suite, run repeatedly on the same machine, produces the same verdict; flakiness attributable to the engine rather than the system under test is effectively zero.
1. **Prove resource safety. **A suite running thousands of iterations returns to baseline memory after each scenario, demonstrating that the collectible-load-context pattern works in practice.
1. **Prove CI fitness. **The CLI runs unattended in a standard CI pipeline and blocks a build on a genuine failure while distinguishing an environment error from a defect.
1. **Generate adoption evidence. **A cohort of pilot teams adopts the tool, authors non-trivial suites, and articulates whether they would pay for cloud execution.

## 4.2 Measurable success criteria

The objectives above are made concrete by the criteria in the table. They are the conditions under which the project is judged to have succeeded and the cloud tier is judged worth funding. Each criterion carries a category that signals what role it plays in the decision: a Gate criterion must be met for the project to declare success; a Guardrail must be met to a minimum bar but does not by itself prove the hypothesis; a Diagnostic is informative but not gating. Stating the category up front prevents the common failure mode where engineering excellence on guardrails papers over a weak demand signal on the gate.

| Criterion | Category | Target for MVP success, with operational definition |
|---|---|---|
| Time to first passing test | Guardrail | A new user authors and runs a guided starter scenario (a single http.rest step against a single dependency) in under 60 minutes, unaided, following the getting-started guide. The full reference scenario — which exercises seeding, secrets, four families, and four providers — is targeted at under 90 minutes with the recipes guide. Measured on at least eight observed onboarding sessions across the pilot cohort. |
| Engine-attributable flakiness | Guardrail | Below 1 in 500 runs across the pilot, measured by repeated execution of a designated stable suite. “Engine-attributable” excludes failures the orchestrator classifies as environment errors or that the system under test produces; the residual category is what the platform itself must keep small. |
| Memory stability | Guardrail | No net memory growth across a 5,000-iteration suite; load contexts demonstrably reclaimed. Measured on the team's own CI on standardised hardware, weekly throughout Phases 2–5. |
| Suite startup time | Diagnostic | A topology of one service plus three dependencies is healthy and ready in under 90 seconds on a typical developer laptop (8-core CPU, 16 GB RAM, NVMe SSD). |
| Sustained pilot adoption | Gate | At least six distinct teams run the tool against a real test suite of theirs at least three times per week for six consecutive weeks, measured by opt-in telemetry (see section 9). At least three of those teams maintain a suite of twenty or more tests across that window. “Team” means a single product engineering team, not a single company; multiple teams within the same company count separately only when they own different services. |
| Behavioural demand signal | Gate | At least four pilot teams sign a non-binding pre-commitment to participate in a paid pilot of the cloud tier at a stated price band (see section 4.4), and at least two pay a small refundable deposit. Stated intent-to-pay alone is not sufficient evidence; the deposit is the behavioural confirmation. |
| Community pathway viability | Gate | At least one external contributor (not a member of the platform team) has a substantial pull request in flight against the Provider SDK within six months of v1.0, with a target of at least one external Verified-tier provider merged within twelve months. At least three additional Community-tier providers exist in the curated index within six months. The realistic six-month signal is active contribution; the merged-Verified signal is twelve-month. Without either, the open-source story the architecture commits to has not been validated, and the recommendation in section 11.3 is to hire a dedicated DevRel role before re-testing. |

*Table 4.1 — Quantified success criteria for the MVP. The Category column makes explicit which criteria are gates for the go/no-go decision and which are guardrails or diagnostics.*

## 4.3 What the success criteria deliberately measure — and do not

The criteria above are designed against a known failure mode: declaring victory on engineering quality (memory, flakiness, startup) while quietly missing on adoption and demand. The categorisation in the table is the safeguard. Engineering hygiene is necessary but not sufficient; a project that meets every guardrail and misses both gates has not validated the hypothesis, and the go/no-go decision in section 11 reflects that. Conversely, a project that hits both gates while a single guardrail is marginally missed should iterate on the guardrail rather than reject the project, because the hypothesis is what is being tested.

Several criteria deserve a word of explanation. “Sustained pilot adoption” is measured behaviourally rather than by survey because stated future use is famously unreliable; six weeks of three-runs-per-week activity is the threshold below which the platform's value has not become routine enough to displace existing habits. “Behavioural demand signal” is the criterion that most directly informs the cloud-tier funding decision, and it deliberately requires money to change hands (even refundably) because intent-to-pay surveys consistently over-state real willingness by a wide margin. “Community pathway viability” is included because the architecture's open-source posture is a strategic bet — the Apache 2.0 Provider SDK, the three-tier governance model, the integration test fixture — and a bet without a payoff measure is just an expense.

## 4.4 The pricing and commercial hypothesis

The MVP is a free local tool with no billing; the go/no-go decision is whether to fund the cloud tier. That decision needs a pricing hypothesis to be testable: “would you pay for cloud execution” is unmoored without a price band. This subsection states the working hypothesis the pilot programme tests. It is a hypothesis intended to be falsified by pilot evidence, not a commitment.

Two axes of pricing are tested in parallel, because pilot conversations indicate that no single axis fits every customer. The seat-priced axis suits organisations where the platform's value attaches to the engineers using it; the consumption-priced axis suits organisations where the value attaches to the CI pipeline running the tests. The plan does not pre-commit to one; it asks pilots to indicate which axis fits their organisation, and the cloud tier launches with both available.

| Tier | Working price hypothesis | Comparator benchmarks |
|---|---|---|
| **Indie** | Free forever. Local execution, the full DSL, the six Core providers, the reporting surface, the VSCode extension. The acquisition surface; the wedge. | Free tier of Postman; the open-source default of xUnit + Testcontainers. |
| **Team — seat-priced** | $25–40 per seat per month for the hosted cross-run dashboard and managed Vault integration, with a bundled quota of cloud-execution container-minutes. Suits teams where most engineers run tests routinely. | Postman Team at $19/seat/month plus add-ons. |
| **Team — consumption-priced** | From $50 per month per organisation as a baseline (covers the hosted dashboard), plus $0.005–0.015 per cloud-execution container-minute, with volume discounts. Suits teams whose primary use is CI rather than individual-developer runs. Both pricing models include the same product surface; the difference is only how the bill is calculated. | GitHub Actions runner pricing of $0.008/minute; CircleCI's per-credit consumption model; Datadog's per-host metering. |
| **Enterprise** | Custom pricing anchored on $150–250 per seat per month with volume discounts, including SSO, on-premises Helm deployment, audit logging, SIEM export, EU/UK data-residency commitments, and a named technical account contact. Consumption priced as in Team. The realistic adoption path for many regulated organisations skips the Team tier entirely and moves from Indie directly to Enterprise, because SSO and on-prem are not optional for them. | Datadog at $15–23/host/month base, GitLab Ultimate at $99/user/month, Snyk Enterprise, Postman Enterprise. |

*Table 4.2 — The working price hypothesis with two parallel Team-tier pricing axes. Pilot teams indicate which axis fits their organisation; the cloud tier launches with both available.*

Four points are worth recording. First, the consumption-metering commitment in the architecture blueprint (section 12.3) was made precisely so that any pricing model the business chooses is supportable by data the engine already collects; the hypothesis above is therefore not constrained by what is measurable. Second, the price bands are deliberately stated as ranges because pilot conversations will refine them — the goal is to fix the order of magnitude, not the exact number. Third, the Indie tier remains free permanently because the wedge depends on frictionless adoption; the cloud tier is the monetisation surface, and the open-source providers are the community-growth surface. The two surfaces are deliberately not in conflict. Fourth, the published feature boundary between the free Indie tier and the paid cloud tier (section 9.7) is part of the project's launch communications, so that the community understands what is and is not commercial before they invest in the open-source providers.

## 4.5 What “success” means in one sentence

> **Success, operationalised**
>
> The MVP has succeeded when at least six pilot teams have used the tool meaningfully for six weeks, at least four have signed a pre-commitment to a paid cloud-tier pilot at the stated price band with at least two backing it by a deposit, at least one external contributor has merged a Verified-tier provider, and the engineering guardrails are all met. Anything short of all three gates is a signal to iterate or reassess before committing to the cloud-tier investment.

# 5. Team and Resourcing

The plan assumes a small, senior, dedicated team rather than a large one. A platform of this kind rewards depth over headcount: the engineering is concentrated in a few hard areas — the Roslyn compiler, the Aspire orchestration, the editor tooling, the provider SDK — and those areas are better served by a few engineers who hold the whole picture than by many who each hold a fragment. The team grew during scoping from six roles to seven so that every workstream defined in section 6 has a named owner; the additional role covers the provider SDK and the reporting surface, which together changed the project's centre of gravity enough to warrant a dedicated owner.

## 5.1 Proposed team

| Role | Count | Principal responsibility | Primary workstreams |
|---|---|---|---|
| Technical lead / architect | 1 | Owns the architecture, the layer contracts, and the hardest design decisions; reviews all significant changes; shares ownership of the compiler workstream. | D (integration); shared B |
| Compiler / runtime engineer | 2 | The YAML-to-CSX compiler, the Roslyn integration, the collectible-load-context memory model, the resilience layer, and the runtime resolution of secret references. | B (compiler), G partially (event-stream emission) |
| Orchestration engineer | 1 | The .NET Aspire integration, container lifecycle, health gating, Respawn-based state reset, and the declarative seed block. | A (orchestration) |
| Extension / tooling engineer | 1 | The VSCode extension, JSON Schema authoring, language-server integration, and the test runner including its selection language, scenario-level parallelism, and isolation contract. | C (authoring tooling) |
| Platform / community engineer | 1 | The Provider SDK, the six Core providers, the CONTRIBUTING.md and integration test fixture, the structured event stream that the reporting surface consumes, the terminal renderer, the HTML report, and the JUnit XML output. | F (Provider SDK) and G (Reporting) |
| Product / delivery lead | 1 | Scope discipline, the pilot programme, success-criteria tracking, stakeholder communication, and migration porting examples. | E (pilot and feedback) |

*Table 5.1 — A seven-person core team for the MVP, with each engineering role mapped to the workstreams of section 6.*

## 5.2 Why this shape

Two of the seven engineers are assigned to the compiler and runtime because that is where the project's deepest technical risk concentrates — dynamic compilation that does not leak memory is genuinely hard, and a single point of failure there would jeopardise the whole plan. Orchestration and extension/tooling each warrant one engineer because, while substantial, they build on mature foundations: Aspire and Testcontainers for the former, the established .NET language server for the latter; the tooling role also absorbs the runner work because the runner shares the same JSON Schema and CLI substrate as the extension. The platform/community engineer is the addition that makes the rest of the plan honest: the Provider SDK plus the reporting surface together are real workstreams, not bullet points, and pretending otherwise would have produced either a missed timeline or a quality compromise on the two surfaces a community contributor and a developer reading a failed test actually touch. The product and delivery lead is not optional overhead; on an MVP, defending the scope boundary against well-intentioned expansion is itself a critical engineering input, and on this MVP the pilot's success depends on the porting examples that role authors.

## 5.3 Skills and assumptions

The plan assumes the team is fluent in modern C# and the .NET 8 LTS ecosystem, comfortable with Docker and container orchestration, and that at least the tooling engineer has prior experience building VSCode extensions and working with the Language Server Protocol. It assumes access to a continuous-integration environment for the team's own pipeline and to a small number of pilot teams willing to adopt an early tool. Because .NET 8 LTS, .NET Aspire, and the surrounding libraries are recent and still evolving, the plan also assumes the team will track upstream preview releases actively rather than pinning to a single version and discovering breaking changes late. For Phase 5's porting examples, the plan assumes the delivery lead has — or can pair with someone with — working familiarity with the testing tools the porting examples target (Postman, k6, xUnit, SpecFlow); if no team member has this familiarity, a short consulting engagement with someone who does is a cheaper way to produce credible porting examples than self-teaching.

## 5.4 Capacities the seven-person team does not include

Two product-shaped capacities are deliberately not staffed inside the seven engineering and delivery roles, and this absence is recorded here rather than left implicit, because both will matter from the moment the platform meets a user.

**Design. **The HTML report, the documentation site, the launch artifacts, the eventual marketing surface — these are user interfaces, and they are sufficiently visible that doing them badly damages the platform's credibility with the audience it most needs to win. The MVP plan does not employ a full-time designer; instead it commits to a part-time engagement (roughly half a day per week, on contract) covering the report's visual treatment, the documentation site's information architecture, and a launch-ready brand kit. The product/delivery lead owns the relationship; if the team cannot secure this engagement, the fallback is to commission specific pieces (report templates, site theme) rather than to skip the work.

**Developer relations. **The community pathway the architecture commits to (Provider SDK under Apache 2.0, three-tier governance, public CONTRIBUTING.md) needs a human face during the launch window: someone who answers GitHub issues quickly, writes the first conference talk, engages on the .NET subreddit and Discord, and converts curiosity into the first wave of community contributions. The MVP plan does not employ a full-time DevRel engineer either; the tech lead and platform/community engineer share this responsibility through the pilot, with an explicit success-criterion gate (Community pathway viability, section 4.2) measuring whether that distribution of effort proves sufficient. If by the three-month post-launch mark the community criterion is not on track, the recommendation in section 11.3's “iterate” outcome includes hiring a dedicated DevRel role.

**An honest note about maintainer load. **Experienced open-source maintainers consistently report that community contribution traffic follows an 80/20 pattern: roughly 80% of issues and pull requests are low-quality (duplicate, off-topic, feature-request-disguised-as-bug, or simply not what the project is for), and the 20% that are substantial are what the strategy depends on. The platform/community engineer's time will, without active discipline, be consumed by triage of the 80% rather than by the substantial 20%. The plan therefore commits to two countermeasures from day one. First, the project publishes a `CONTRIBUTING.md` with explicit scope guardrails and an issue-template set that auto-closes off-topic submissions politely (linking to the relevant alternative project). Second, the platform/community engineer is given an explicit triage budget of one half-day per week ringfenced for the first six months; if community traffic exceeds that budget repeatedly, the trigger is to hire DevRel, not to absorb the load silently. The community gate in section 4.2 measures the substantial 20%; if the team is drowning in the 80% they cannot ship to the substantial 20%, and the plan refuses to pretend otherwise.

**The first thirty days post-launch are explicitly resourced. **Open-source projects either signal seriousness in their first month or they do not, and the launch plan in section 9.4 commits to: every GitHub issue receives a first response within one business day; every external pull request receives a first response within five business days; the platform/community engineer is the named point of contact and the tech lead is the named backup. The product/delivery lead owns the schedule and intervenes if the response-time commitment is at risk. “Whoever sees it first” is explicitly not the model; ambiguity on this is what kills early communities.

## 5.5 Stakeholder map and communication rhythm

Twenty-four weeks of work for a seven-person team is a substantial investment, and the people funding it deserve to be brought along rather than surprised at the go/no-go gate. This subsection names the stakeholders the plan accounts for and the cadence at which they hear from the project.

| Stakeholder | Interest | What they receive, and how often |
|---|---|---|
| Executive sponsor | Approves funding, owns the go/no-go decision. | Monthly written update from the delivery lead (one page: progress, criteria status, risks moved, asks); a structured steering review at every phase boundary. |
| Engineering leadership | Owns engineering quality, headcount, and integration with the wider engineering function. | Bi-weekly demo and walkthrough led by the tech lead; access to the team's CI dashboard; an invitation to all phase-exit reviews. |
| Finance partner | Tracks spend against approved budget; will fund the cloud tier if go/no-go signals Go. | Monthly burn-rate and remaining-budget snapshot alongside the executive update; an early conversation in Phase 3 about the cloud-tier funding envelope so a Go decision can move quickly. |
| Security and compliance reviewers | Sign-off for any data or credential handling, especially for enterprise readiness. | An early conversation in Phase 1 to set expectations; security checklist artifacts in Phases 2 and 4; full review before any pilot involves real data. |
| Pilot teams | Use the product, generate the evidence the go/no-go decision rests on. | Weekly working session per team during the pilot; structured retrospective at week three; demand-signal conversation at week six. Full pilot programme design in section 8.5. |
| The wider .NET community | Eventual adopters, contributors, and amplifiers; the community-pathway gate depends on them. | First contact at v1.0 launch through the channels named in section 9.4; ongoing engagement via the Provider SDK contribution loop and a recurring (monthly) public update. |

*Table 5.2 — Stakeholder map and communication cadence.*

The delivery lead owns the rhythm. The most important entry in the table is the first one: monthly written updates to the executive sponsor are the single biggest determinant of whether funding stays in place through a project's middle weeks, and an MVP that depends on a go/no-go decision in week 24 must keep the decision-maker informed continuously rather than only at the end.

# 6. Technical Workstreams

Before laying out a timeline, it helps to name the parallel streams of work that the timeline sequences. The MVP decomposes into seven workstreams. They are not strictly independent — the timeline in section 7 sequences their dependencies — but each has a coherent owner and a coherent definition of done.

## 6.1 Workstream A — Orchestration foundation

This workstream delivers the ability to provision a microservice topology locally and hand the test code a set of healthy, discovered endpoints. It covers programmatic Aspire AppHost construction, the .WaitFor and health-gate startup logic, the build-once-per-suite fixture, and Respawn-based state reset. It also owns the data lifecycle's other half: the declarative seed block that establishes reference state after the topology is healthy and before the first step runs, applied inside the same health-gated lifecycle so a failed seed is an environment error rather than a confusing assertion failure. It is sequenced first because every other workstream needs something to test against, and a stub topology lets the others begin before the workstream is fully complete.

## 6.2 Workstream B — Compiler and runtime

This is the deepest workstream. It delivers the YAML parser, the AST, schema validation, CSX code generation for the six Core providers, and the Roslyn compilation pipeline. Critically, it delivers the memory model: the compile-once pattern, the collectible `AssemblyLoadContext`, and explicit unloading. It also delivers the resilience layer behind `verifyMode: RETRY` and the variable-capture mechanism. The compilation pipeline is provider-mediated by design — the resolve, bind, validate, and emit stages flow through the contract owned by workstream F — so the two workstreams must agree on the contract early in phase 1 and the compiler must be exercised against multiple Core providers before phase 4 begins. This workstream also owns secret resolution: the ${secret:…} reference syntax, its pluggable sources (environment variables and Vault for the MVP), and the redaction hook that the reporting workstream consumes so that a resolved secret never reaches a report. Because the memory model is both the hardest and the highest-risk element, the plan front-loads a proof of concept for it in phase one rather than discovering problems near the end.

## 6.3 Workstream C — Authoring tooling

This workstream delivers the developer-facing surface: the VSCode extension with schema-driven YAML support, embedded C# IntelliSense via the .NET language server, and the headless CLI runner. The runner is more than an executor: this workstream owns its selection language (by tag, ownership, path, and change-set), its scenario-level parallelism bounded by a concurrency budget, the per-scenario isolation contract, and a watch mode for fast local iteration. It depends on the JSON Schema being stable, so its heavier work is sequenced after the schema settles in workstream B.

## 6.4 Workstream D — Integration and hardening

This workstream is where the others converge. It delivers the end-to-end reference scenario running across all six Core providers, the verdict taxonomy and reporting surface in their final form, the telemetry signals needed to distinguish a defect from an environment failure, and a memory-leak detection test that runs in the team's own CI. It cannot complete until A, B, C, F, and G are substantially done.

## 6.5 Workstream E — Pilot and feedback

This workstream is not code; it is the deliberate collection of the evidence the MVP exists to produce. It covers recruiting pilot teams, onboarding them, instrumenting the success criteria, gathering structured feedback, and producing the demand-signal assessment that informs the decision in section 11. It runs in parallel with late development so that feedback can still influence the first release.

## 6.6 Workstream F — Provider SDK and Core provider set

This workstream owns the source-level extension model: the C# contract that providers implement, the reflection-based registry that discovers them at startup, the JSON Schema composition that lets the editor see them, and the six Core providers shipped under Apache 2.0 alongside the engine. It is separated from the compiler workstream because its definition of done is different: the compiler is finished when the engine compiles and runs; the SDK is finished when an outside contributor can implement a new provider without help, validated by an end-to-end dry run before pilot. The CONTRIBUTING.md document, the worked example provider from the architecture blueprint, and the integration test fixture that every Verified-tier provider must pass are all delivered here. By publishing this surface alongside v1.0, the project shifts the long tail of database, broker, and protocol support from a platform-team obligation to an open-source contribution path that the community can grow at its own pace.

## 6.7 Workstream G — Result reporting and diagnostics

This workstream owns the surface through which the platform's outcome reaches the developer, the CI system, the team lead, and the auditor. It is its own workstream rather than a Phase 4 bullet because reporting is the platform's user interface in the literal sense: every other workstream's value is realised only when its outcome becomes legible to a human reader, and a testing tool that reports badly is a testing tool that nobody trusts. The workstream delivers the structured JSON-Lines event stream every renderer consumes, the rich terminal renderer with the polling timeline and the captured-variable thread, the HTML report written to disk with the reproducibility envelope embedded, JUnit XML for CI gates, and the VSCode Test Explorer integration. It also defines the IStepDiffRenderer contract that providers in workstream F implement so that the report rendering of a failed db-assert.postgres step is faithful to relational data, the rendering of a failed db-assert.mongodb step to document data, and so on. The workstream begins in Phase 1 with the event-stream schema and a minimal terminal renderer used by the compiler workstream's own integration tests, and it completes in Phase 4 with the full surface ready for pilot.

# 7. Phased Roadmap and Timeline

The MVP is planned as five sequential phases spanning roughly twenty-four weeks. The phases are sequential in their centre of gravity but overlap at the edges: a later phase's low-risk preparation begins while an earlier phase finishes. Each phase ends with a concrete, demonstrable milestone, because a phase that cannot be demonstrated cannot be honestly called complete.

## 7.1 Phase overview

| Phase | Weeks | Theme | Exit milestone |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Foundations** | 1–4 | De-risk the hardest unknowns. | Roslyn compile-once memory model proven; a stub topology starts and is health-gated; the provider contract is drafted and reviewed; the structured event-stream schema is drafted. |
| **2. Core compiler** | 5–10 | The DSL compiles and runs. | Three Core providers (http.rest, db-assert.postgres, script.csharp) execute end to end against a real topology through the provider-mediated pipeline; declarative seeding and environment-variable secret resolution work; a minimal terminal renderer reads the event stream. |
| **3. Full step set** | 11–16 | Complete the language. | All six Core providers and RETRY mode working; schema frozen for v1; Provider SDK and CONTRIBUTING.md published in draft; runner selection, parallelism, and the Vault secret source land; the polling timeline and captured-variable thread render in the terminal. |
| **4. Tooling and hardening** | 17–21 | Make it usable and trustworthy. | VSCode extension and CLI feature-complete; reference scenario green; memory-leak test in CI; Provider SDK dry-run; HTML report and JUnit XML feature-complete; CI templates and the documentation set published. |
| **5. Pilot and release** | 22–24 | Put it in real hands. | Pilot cohort onboarded; success criteria measured; v1.0 released; demand signal assessed; community provider repository opened for contributions. |

*Table 7.1 — The five phases of the MVP, with exit milestones.*

## 7.2 Why this ordering

The sequence is governed by risk, not by the order in which features are most visible. Phase one tackles the two unknowns most capable of derailing the project — whether dynamic compilation can be made memory-safe, and whether Aspire orchestration behaves predictably — because discovering a fundamental problem in week three is recoverable and discovering it in week twenty is not. Phases two and three build the language outward from a proven core. Phase four deliberately separates hardening from feature work, so that usability and trustworthiness are treated as deliverables rather than as whatever time remains. Phase five is kept distinct because gathering evidence is a real activity that needs real time, not a footnote to development.

> **Planning note**
>
> The twenty-four-week estimate is a planning figure for a seven-person team working without major interruption. It is offered to size the effort and sequence the risks, not as a commitment. The phase exit milestones, not the calendar, are the true measure of progress: a phase is done when its milestone is demonstrable, whatever week that falls in.

# 8. Detailed Phase Breakdown

This section expands each phase into its principal tasks and states the entry assumption and exit criterion. The tasks are described at the level a delivery lead needs to track progress; the engineering detail behind them lives in the architecture and specification documents.

## 8.1 Phase 1 — Foundations (weeks 1–4)

The first phase exists to convert the project's two largest uncertainties into either confidence or an early, cheap course correction.

- **Memory-model proof of concept. **Build a minimal Roslyn pipeline that compiles a trivial script once, runs it many thousands of times inside a collectible load context, unloads, and demonstrates memory returning to baseline. This is the single most important task in the plan.
- **Provider-closure memory test. **Extend the memory proof of concept to run against the full transitive closure of every Core provider's dependencies — Npgsql, Confluent.Kafka, MongoDB.Driver, StackExchange.Redis, and their transitive packages — not just against a trivial script. Static state held in library singletons (HttpClient handler pools, Npgsql connection pools, Confluent producer caches, OpenTelemetry tracers) can pin objects across the collectible-load-context boundary; only a closure-level test catches that, and discovering it at Phase 4 would force a costly rework. This regression test becomes a permanent CI gate.
- **Orchestration spike. **Stand up a stub topology — one service, one database — through a programmatic Aspire AppHost, with health-gated startup, and confirm that endpoints resolve reliably through service discovery.
- **Provider contract draft. **Write the C# interfaces (IStepProvider, IStepBinder, IStepValidator, IStepCompiler, IResourceContributor) and a throwaway reference provider that exercises the full lifecycle, so the compiler workstream can build against a stable contract from the start of phase 2.
- **Event-stream schema draft. **Define the structured JSON-Lines event schema that every renderer and the Healer agent will consume, including step-started, step-attempt, step-completed, and scenario-completed events. A minimal terminal renderer reading this stream becomes the compiler workstream's own integration-test surface from phase 2, which means reporting is exercised continuously rather than designed in isolation.
- **Schema first draft. **Draft the JSON Schema for the four top-level sections and the http.rest provider fragment, enough to unblock tooling work in later phases and to demonstrate the schema composition mechanism on a single provider.
- **Engineering CI. **Establish the team's own build pipeline, into which the memory-leak detection test will later be wired.
**Exit criterion. **The memory model is demonstrably sound, the stub topology starts reliably, and the provider contract has been exercised end to end by a reference provider. If any of these is in doubt, the plan pauses here for a design correction rather than carrying the risk forward.

## 8.2 Phase 2 — Core compiler (weeks 5–10)

The second phase makes the language real for the first time, deliberately limited to three Core providers so that the full compile-and-run path is exercised through the provider-mediated pipeline before breadth is added.

- **YAML parser and AST. **Parse a test file into the Abstract Syntax Tree and validate it against the phase-one schema.
- **Three Core providers. **Implement http.rest, db-assert.postgres, and script.csharp — chosen because together they exercise requests, assertions, and the escape hatch, and because each lives in its own assembly so the registry's source-level discovery is genuinely tested.
- **Provider-mediated CSX generation. **Promote the phase-one provider contract into the production compiler: resolve, bind, validate, plan resources, and emit, with each Core provider contributing its own CSX fragment.
- **Roslyn pipeline in production form. **Promote the phase-one proof of concept into the real compiler, with the global-context object and dynamic assembly resolution.
- **Variable capture (first form). **JSONPath extraction and brace substitution, sufficient to thread a value from an http.rest step into a db-assert.postgres step.
- **Aspire orchestration (production form). **Promote the spike into the real orchestration layer with build-once fixtures and Respawn reset.
- **Declarative seeding and secret resolution. **Deliver the environment.seed block for reference SQL and document fixtures, and the ${secret:…} resolution with the environment-variable source. These land in phase 2 because a realistic test of the three Core providers needs both seeded reference data and a way to supply a credential without inlining it.
- **Minimal terminal renderer. **Build the first version of the report renderer reading the structured event stream, sufficient to show step verdicts and basic durations. Using this renderer as the compiler workstream's primary feedback surface ensures the event-stream schema is exercised in anger from this phase forward, rather than retro-fitted in phase 4.
**Exit criterion. **A test file using http.rest, db-assert.postgres, and script.csharp compiles and runs end to end against a real local topology, with reference data seeded, a credential supplied through a secret reference, state threaded between steps, the provider registry discovering each provider via reflection at startup, and the minimal terminal renderer displaying per-step verdicts.

## 8.3 Phase 3 — Full step set (weeks 11–16)

The third phase completes the language so that the reference scenario can be expressed in full, and prepares the open-source surface that turns the long tail of provider work into a community contribution path.

- **Three more Core providers. **mq-publish.kafka and mq-expect.kafka with schema-registry and Avro support, plus webhook-listen.http with its ephemeral local listener.
- **RETRY verification mode. **The Polly-backed bounded exponential-backoff polling behind verifyMode: RETRY, working across mq-expect.kafka, db-assert.postgres, and webhook-listen.http.
- **XPath capture and full substitution. **Complete the variable mechanism across all step kinds and result formats.
- **Freeze the v1 schema. **Finalise the JSON Schema for the first release so that tooling can build against a stable contract; freeze the provider contract at the same time.
- **Publish the Provider SDK. **Release the C# contract as a NuGet package, write CONTRIBUTING.md, document the integration test fixture every Verified provider must pass, and publish the worked example provider from the architecture blueprint as a public reference. Invite a small number of pre-pilot contributors to attempt their first community provider against this surface.
- **Begin pilot recruitment. **Open the recruitment channels named in section 8.5.1 — direct outreach, .NET community posts, conference talk submission. The lead time from cold outreach to engaged pilot team is six to ten weeks in practice, so Phase 3 is the latest point at which recruitment can begin if the Phase 5 cohort is to land on time.
- **Choose the product name and incorporate the vendor entity. **The product name decision unblocks the docs URL, the GitHub organisation, the package names on NuGet and the VSCode Marketplace, and the launch artifacts. The vendor entity incorporation is what makes the platform a thing enterprise procurement teams can record rights from, even for the free Indie tier. Both are Phase 3 deliverables so that Phase 4's documentation and CI templates can be produced under the chosen name, and so that the trademark application is filed early in Phase 4. Legal advice in this phase confirms the jurisdiction and the entity structure.
- **Polling timeline and captured-variable thread. **Extend the terminal renderer with the two rendering features that most directly repay the platform's asynchronous-first design: the per-attempt polling timeline for RETRY steps, and the captured-variable thread that shows where each value in a scenario originated. Define the IStepDiffRenderer contract so providers can supply faithful expected-versus-observed rendering for their data model.
- **Runner selection, parallelism, and the Vault secret source. **Deliver the runner's selection language (tag, ownership, path, change-set), scenario-level parallelism with the concurrency budget and the per-scenario isolation contract, and the Vault secret source alongside the environment-variable source from phase 2. These turn a single-suite executor into a runner that scales to a real test estate.
**Exit criterion. **All six Core providers work, RETRY behaves deterministically, the schema is frozen for v1, the Provider SDK has been validated by at least one outside contributor implementing a non-Core provider end to end, the terminal renderer shows the polling timeline and captured-variable thread, and the runner can select and parallelise a multi-file suite.

## 8.4 Phase 4 — Tooling and hardening (weeks 17–21)

The fourth phase turns a working engine into a product a stranger can use and trust.

- **VSCode extension. **Schema-driven YAML autocomplete and validation, and embedded C# IntelliSense in script steps via the .NET language server.
- **CLI runner. **The headless runner with deterministic exit codes and CI-friendly output.
- **Reporting surface to feature-complete. **Promote the terminal renderer to its final form, deliver the standalone HTML report with the reproducibility envelope embedded, finalise JUnit XML output for CI gates, and integrate with the VSCode Test Explorer so failures decorate the right YAML line. The reporting surface is the platform's user interface and should be treated as the deliverable that determines whether the pilot succeeds.
- **Reporting and verdict taxonomy. **Per-step results distinguishing pass, fail, environment error, and inconclusive verdicts, surfaced consistently across the terminal, the HTML report, JUnit XML, and the editor.
- **Memory-leak test in CI. **Wire the phase-one memory check into the team's pipeline as a permanent regression guard.
- **Provider SDK dry-run. **Walk an outside contributor through implementing a non-Core provider end to end against the v1 SDK, treating any friction as a documentation or contract bug. The dry-run gives the team early evidence that the contribution path the platform's open-source story depends on actually works.
- **CI/CD integration templates. **Ship at least a GitHub Actions reusable workflow and a GitLab CI template that invoke the runner, gate on its exit code, and attach the HTML report and JUnit XML as build artifacts. The CLI reaches developers through their pipeline, so a turnkey template materially lowers the adoption barrier.
- **Documentation set. **Beyond a getting-started guide: a recipes collection (seeding patterns, test doubles with WireMock, secret sources), a common-patterns guide, and a troubleshooting cookbook. The 'time to first passing test under 60 minutes' success criterion depends directly on this, so documentation is a phase-4 deliverable rather than a pilot-time scramble.
**Exit criterion. **The reference scenario is green from the editor and the CLI; the extension is feature-complete for the MVP; memory safety is continuously verified; an outside contributor has implemented a non-Core provider against the SDK without platform-team help; and a CI template runs the suite and publishes its report.

## 8.5 Phase 5 — Pilot and release (weeks 22–24)

The final phase gathers the evidence the whole MVP exists to produce. It is the phase most often underestimated, because pilot programmes look like coordination work but in practice are product work — onboarding rituals, weekly engagement, structured retrospectives, and the rigorous translation of conversation into evidence. The subsections below specify the pilot programme rather than gesturing at it.

### 8.5.1 The pilot programme design

Eight teams are recruited to give a comfortable margin over the six-team success criterion. Recruitment begins in Phase 3, before the tool is ready, because the lead time on landing engaged pilot teams from cold outreach is six to ten weeks in practice. Channels run in parallel: direct outreach to engineers in the platform team's professional network and prior employers; targeted posts on the .NET subreddit, the .NET Foundation Slack, and the dotnet Discord; a Show HN / Lobsters post that links to the worked reference scenario; and one conference talk submitted to a .NET-focused event timed near the launch window.

The pilot runs on two tracks because the commitment a sixty-engineer fintech startup can make is different from what a regulated enterprise can. Teams self-select into the track that fits them, and the success criteria's behavioural signals apply equally to both — a pilot is judged on what its engineers actually do, not on what their formal process looks like.

| Track | Commitment | Cadence | Best fit |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Engaged** | One engineer-day per week for six weeks; attendance at all weekly working sessions; permission to be named in release notes; structured retrospectives at week three and six. | Weekly synchronous working session; structured retrospectives; demand-signal conversation at week six. | Mid-to-large organisations and any pilot team prepared to invest seriously in evaluating the tool. |
| **Light-touch** | No fixed weekly commitment; activity opt-in; anonymous credit only by default; structured retrospective at week six only. | Async Discord channel; bi-weekly written update from the platform team; a single end-of-pilot conversation that doubles as the demand-signal interview. | Startup teams (under fifty engineers) where dedicating an engineer-day per week to evaluation is not feasible. Reduces the selection bias toward big-company pilots. |

Pilot teams of either track must meet a profile: a .NET microservices estate of at least five services, at least one team member with the platform engineer or staff engineer profile described in section 2.1, an existing integration testing pain point they can articulate, and willingness to opt into telemetry for the duration. Teams that do not meet the profile are gratefully declined.

The pilot contract is symmetric. The platform team commits to early access, the agreed cadence for the chosen track, direct support through the agreed channel, prompt issue triage (response within one business day, fix or workaround within five), and a written acknowledgment of the team's contribution in the v1.0 release notes (named for engaged-track teams, anonymous for light-touch). The pilot team commits to at least three runs of their own tests per week, the retrospective cadence of the chosen track, and permission to use their experience in launch communications (named or anonymous per their track). Both parties can exit cleanly at any time; a pilot that disengages is a data point about the tool, not a failure of the team.

### 8.5.2 Support, geography, and language

Pilot support runs on a private Slack channel per team plus a shared GitHub issue tracker, with a business-hours response commitment from the platform team during the pilot window. “Business hours” is European working hours (08:00–18:00 CET) because the platform team is Europe-based; pilot teams in other timezones are accepted but the time-zone overlap is acknowledged up front rather than discovered later. The working language of the pilot is English; pilot teams whose engineers do not work fluently in English are not excluded but receive an explicit warning that the tooling, documentation, and conversations are English-only at v1.0.

### 8.5.3 Pilot data collection and the demand-signal conversation

Three streams of evidence are collected through the pilot. First, opt-in telemetry from the running tool itself — number of runs, suite sizes, verdicts, time-to-first-passing-test — captured against the success criteria in section 4.2. Second, structured retrospectives at week three (calibration: is the tool meeting expectations?) and week six (the demand-signal conversation: at what price band would you use the cloud tier?). Third, observational notes from the weekly working sessions, which often surface friction the telemetry cannot see. Each pilot's evidence is summarised in a written brief no later than the end of week 24, and the briefs together feed the go/no-go assessment in section 11.3.

### 8.5.4 Phase 5 deliverables

- **Onboard the pilot cohort. **Bring at least eight teams onto the tool using the Phase 4 documentation and the support model in 8.5.2.
- **Run weekly working sessions. **One hour per team per week, owned by the delivery lead, with a structured agenda (last week's runs, this week's blockers, this week's planned tests).
- **Author migration porting examples. **Most pilot teams already own integration tests. Author worked examples that port a representative Postman collection, an xUnit integration test, and a SpecFlow feature onto the platform, showing the script step as the escape hatch for assertion logic teams want to keep. The honest message is that existing tests are re-authored rather than auto-converted, and these examples make that path concrete rather than daunting.
- **Instrument and measure. **Collect the section 4 success criteria — time to first test, flakiness, adoption, behavioural demand signal, community pathway viability — by telemetry, retrospective, and observation per 8.5.3.
- **Release v1.0. **Publish the first stable version and the VSCode extension through the channels specified in the launch plan (section 9.4).
- **Assess the gates. **Produce the written assessment that feeds the go / no-go decision on the cloud tier in section 11.3, with each gate criterion explicitly addressed.
**Exit criterion. **v1.0 is released; eight pilot teams have completed at least the six-week active window; the success criteria in section 4.2 have been measured against their targets with each gate addressed explicitly; and a clear, evidence-backed recommendation on the cloud tier is documented and ready for the steering review.

# 9. Release, Launch, and Operations

Building the product is half the work; getting it into the hands of the right developers, in the right shape, with the right policies around it, is the other half. This section specifies the operational scaffolding of v1.0: how it is distributed, how it is documented, how it is launched, what data it collects, how it stays accessible and internationalisable, and the open-source licence stance that the architecture commits to but the plan must operationalise.

## 9.1 The release manifest

A new pilot user, on day one, must answer half a dozen practical questions before they can run a test: what do I install, on what operating system, from where, with what dependencies, under what licence, with what telemetry policy? The release manifest below states the platform's commitments. Each row is a concrete v1.0 deliverable and an explicit constraint on what the team must produce by the end of Phase 4.

| Concern | v1.0 commitment |
|---|---|
| Supported platforms | Windows 10/11, macOS 13+ (Apple Silicon and Intel), and Ubuntu/Debian-class Linux (kernel 5.10+). Other Linux distributions work but are not tested in CI. |
| Required dependencies | Docker Desktop or Docker Engine 24+, .NET 8 LTS SDK or runtime, and an MS-Windows or Unix-like terminal. VSCode 1.85+ for the extension. No other prerequisites at v1.0. |
| Distribution channels | Primary: the dotnet global tool channel (dotnet tool install -g) for the CLI; the VSCode Marketplace for the extension. Secondary: a signed .msi for Windows, a notarised .pkg for macOS, and a .deb for Debian-family Linux, all attached to GitHub Releases. |
| Licence | Apache 2.0 for the engine, the Provider SDK, and the six Core providers (the Indie tier). The licence is displayed at first-run and accepted implicitly by use; no click-through EULA at v1.0. |
| Update model | Manual at v1.0: the user runs dotnet tool update or installs a new release. The tool checks for updates at most once per day and prints a one-line notice when one exists; it does not auto-update. Automatic update is a post-MVP enhancement. |
| Signing and provenance | All binaries are signed (Authenticode on Windows, Apple Developer ID on macOS, GPG-signed packages on Linux). The release artifacts include SBOMs and provenance attestations to make supply-chain verification straightforward. |
| Telemetry | Opt-in only at v1.0 (see section 9.3). The tool prints an explicit notice at first run, and runs in a no-telemetry default until the user opts in. No telemetry is collected from runs against systems flagged as production. |

*Table 9.1 — The v1.0 release manifest. Each commitment is a Phase 4 deliverable.*

## 9.2 Documentation as a product surface

For a developer tool, the documentation is not collateral; it is the first product surface a prospective user touches and often the surface against which the decision to adopt is made. The MVP treats documentation as a product deliverable with its own success criterion and its own structure rather than as a phase-end scramble.

The information architecture covers five layers, each addressed at a different reader: a single-page “get started in 60 minutes” guided tour for the first-time visitor; a recipes collection (seeding patterns, test doubles, secret sources, common CI integrations) for the user who has the basics and wants the next thing; a comprehensive language reference auto-generated from the unified JSON Schema so it cannot drift; a provider-by-provider reference assembled from each provider's README and schema fragment; and a troubleshooting cookbook of the failure modes the platform team has seen during development and pilot.

Documentation is hosted on a dedicated subdomain (docs.<productname>.dev once the product name is chosen in Phase 3), versioned alongside the engine and the schema, served from a static site backed by a Git-hosted source. The success criterion is operationalised: in at least eighty percent of observed onboarding sessions, the pilot user reaches their first passing test using only the published docs, without contacting the platform team. Failures of this criterion are catalogued and become Phase 5 hotfix targets to the docs themselves.

## 9.3 Telemetry, privacy, and feedback

Pilot evidence depends on knowing what users actually did, not only on what they say. The MVP collects opt-in telemetry from the running tool, with the stance set deliberately to favour privacy at the cost of completeness; the alternative — default-on collection — would harvest more data but cost trust that the platform cannot afford to spend at this stage.

The opt-in flow is straightforward. At first run the tool prints a notice describing what telemetry would be collected, the URL where the full policy is published, and the command to enable it. Nothing is collected until the user runs that command. When telemetry is on, the tool reports: count of runs, count of scenarios per run, counts of verdicts by category, count of steps by family and provider, suite startup time, time-to-first-passing-test on a fresh install, the user's anonymous installation id, and the platform and tool version. The tool does not report: test file contents, captured variable values, secret references or resolved values, error messages, system-under-test addresses, container image names, or any data that originated from the system under test. A test file may declare itself non-telemetered with a metadata flag, in which case no run-level telemetry is reported from that file.

Telemetry data flows to a small backend the platform team operates for the pilot duration (and which becomes part of the cloud tier if the project proceeds). It is retained for ninety days at the Indie tier and is never shared with third parties. Users can disable telemetry at any time, and disabling deletes the installation id from the backend within thirty days. Structured feedback during the pilot — the weekly working sessions, the week-three and week-six retrospectives — is captured in the delivery lead's notes rather than through the tool, and is treated as confidential to the pilot.

## 9.4 Launch

v1.0 is a deliberate launch, not a quiet release, because the open-source community pathway depends on the platform being visible to the .NET developer community on day one. The launch artifact is the worked reference scenario from the DSL specification, rendered as a short demo and a written walkthrough, because a concrete example travels further than feature lists.

| Channel | Launch-day artifact |
|---|---|
| Project website | The reference scenario as a written walkthrough; the get-started guide; the Provider SDK CONTRIBUTING.md; download and install instructions for all three operating systems. |
| GitHub | v1.0 release tagged, with binaries, SBOM, and provenance attached; CONTRIBUTING.md, CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md, and SECURITY.md present; first batch of “good first issue” labels open for community contributors. |
| Hacker News / Lobsters | A Show HN post pointing to the website, framing the platform around the reference scenario rather than around features. |
| Reddit /r/dotnet | A discussion post inviting questions; the platform team commits to answering for the first 24 hours. |
| .NET Foundation Slack and dotnet Discord | Announcement in the relevant channels by the tech lead, with an offer to demo for any team that wants one. |
| Conference talk | If scheduled, the launch-week talk doubles as the launch event for the relevant audience. |
| Blog post | A long-form launch post on the platform's blog walking through the design choices, the asynchronous-first reporting layer, and the community provider model. |

*Table 9.2 — Launch-day channels and the artifact carried on each.*

The first thirty days after launch are owned by the tech lead and the platform/community engineer jointly. They commit to: responding to every GitHub issue within one business day; merging or responding to every external pull request within five business days; engaging actively in the threads on Hacker News, Reddit, and Discord; and producing a second blog post at the two-week mark addressing the most common questions and the most interesting community contributions to date. The launch is judged successful if, by day thirty, at least two external contributors have opened pull requests against the providers repository and the platform team has not visibly fallen behind on responses.

## 9.5 Accessibility and internationalisation

**Accessibility. **The HTML report and the VSCode extension are user surfaces and the MVP commits to WCAG 2.1 AA conformance at v1.0. Concretely: the verdict colour scheme is paired with shape and text indicators so that the four verdicts remain distinguishable to colour-blind users; the report is keyboard-navigable end to end with a logical tab order; semantic HTML is used (headings, lists, tables) rather than div-soup; and the terminal renderer continues to work in screen-reader-friendly minimal mode (the --no-decorations flag). The team commissions one accessibility review during Phase 4 as part of the documentation engagement.

**Internationalisation. **v1.0 is English-only across the tool, the documentation, the error messages, and the launch communications. The codebase is structured so that user-facing strings are localisable rather than literal where it costs little to do so, but no second language is translated for v1.0. The post-MVP roadmap (section 11.3) names i18n as a deferred capability whose priority depends on geographic adoption patterns observed during the pilot.

## 9.6 Open-source licence, governance, and trademark

The architecture blueprint commits the engine, the Provider SDK, and the six Core providers to Apache 2.0 under the Indie tier. The plan operationalises three follow-ons that the licence choice implies.

**Contributor agreement. **Contributors sign off via the Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO) rather than a Contributor Licence Agreement. The DCO is the lighter-weight choice, requires no separate signing infrastructure, integrates with GitHub through a standard bot, and is consistent with the .NET Foundation's own practice. A heavier CLA would be appropriate only if the project later relicenses or dual-licenses; that decision is deferred past the MVP.

**Trademark. **Once the product name is chosen in Phase 3, the project files a trademark application in the team's home jurisdiction (Czech Republic / EUIPO) covering the relevant Nice classifications for software and SaaS. The Apache 2.0 licence does not protect the name, and a hostile fork using the same name is a real risk if the project succeeds; the trademark is the inexpensive insurance against it. A drafted trademark policy is published at v1.0 launch (section 9.9), not after the first hostile use — hostile uses arrive faster than trademark filings issue, and the published policy is what gives the project a defensible stance from day one.

**Governance of the community providers. **The three-tier governance model in the architecture (Core, Verified, Community) is operationalised by a small written governance document at v1.0 launch covering: who decides what goes into Core (the platform team); who decides what is Verified (the published rubric below); how Verified-tier provider authors gain commit rights to the providers repository (after their third merged PR); and how disputes are resolved. The model deliberately keeps decision authority with the platform team during v1.0 so that the community quality bar is set; broader governance models (a foundation, elected stewards) are appropriate later if the project's scale warrants them.

The Verified-tier promotion rubric is published as a checklist, not as prose, because checklists drive behaviour and prose drifts. The minimum bar:

- The provider's integration-test fixture passes on the official matrix (the engine's main, plus the two preceding minor versions).
