- The provider's README contains worked examples covering at least three realistic use cases and a known-limitations section.
- The security checklist is signed off: credential handling reviewed for correctness, transitive dependency vulnerabilities scanned (zero high-severity at promotion), TLS defaults inspected, no telemetry phoning home, package signature verified.
- The licence is Apache 2.0 (or compatible) and the contributor has signed off via DCO.
- The provider declares a MinEngineVersion compatible with the engine's current major version.
- At least one platform-team maintainer has read the emitted CSX for the provider's representative steps and confirmed it follows the CsxFragment composition contract in the architecture blueprint's section 13.3.1.
Authors whose provider does not yet meet the rubric remain in the Community tier with no implied endorsement, and the rubric itself is the actionable feedback for what needs work. Publishing the rubric — rather than leaving it to maintainer judgement — is what makes the gate fair, defensible against accusations of bias, and durable across maintainer turnover.

## 9.7 The published feature boundary between the open-source and commercial tiers

Open-source projects with commercial tiers consistently stumble on the same trap: the community discovers, over time, that the commercial tier has features they want, asks for those features in the open-source tier, are told no, and the goodwill curdles. The platform forestalls this by publishing the feature boundary explicitly at launch, in writing, on the project website, before anyone asks. The boundary is part of the project's first-day communications, not a discovery the community makes later.

| Surface | Tier |
|---|---|
| The engine, the YAML DSL, the six Core providers, the Provider SDK, the VSCode extension, the terminal renderer, the HTML report, the JUnit XML output, the structured event stream, the CLI runner, the secret-reference resolution mechanism, the reproducibility envelope. | Apache 2.0, Indie tier, free permanently. |
| The hosted cross-run dashboard, managed Vault integration, the cloud execution fabric (Testcontainer-Cloud-style remote provisioning), the agentic Planner / Generator / Healer, the Performance LAB, run-history retention beyond the local cache, organisational analytics. | Commercial, Team tier and above. These surfaces have always been intended as the cloud value layered above the open-source engine. |
| SSO / OIDC federation, on-premises Helm deployment, audit-logging, SIEM export, EU/UK data-residency commitments, named technical-account contact, dedicated support SLA. | Commercial, Enterprise tier. |

*Table 9.3 — The feature boundary between the open-source and commercial tiers, published at launch on the project website. The Indie tier is permanently free; the cloud value is in the upper tiers.*

## 9.8 The public roadmap

A one-page public roadmap is published on the project website at v1.0 launch, derived from the internal phased plan but written for an external audience. It names the next two minor releases (what they include, what they deliberately do not, target dates given as quarters rather than weeks), and a separate section names a small set of capabilities that are deliberately not on the roadmap, so the community can either contribute them via the Provider SDK or build them externally without waiting. The roadmap is updated at every minor release. Transparency on the roadmap is what builds the trust that the community pathway depends on — contributors will not invest in a project whose direction they cannot see, and the architecture and project-plan documents are not the right artifact for this because they are too long and too internal-facing.

## 9.9 The published trademark policy

The trademark filing alone does not protect the project; the published policy does, because the policy is what the community and any potential infringer can read in advance. The policy is drafted before v1.0 launch and published on the project website at the same time as the launch announcement, not in response to the first dispute. Following the template successful .NET-ecosystem and Apache-Foundation projects use, the policy covers:

- Names and logos may be used to refer to the project factually — in articles, talks, comparisons, integration documentation — without permission. This is the explicit grant the community needs to talk about the project freely.
- Use of the name or logo to identify products, services, distributions, or forks requires written permission. This includes “TestPlatform Plus”, “TestPlatform Pro”, and similar derivative names.
- Community projects, training materials, and conference talks may use the name and logo with attribution, without permission.
- The platform will pursue confusing uses through appropriate legal channels; serious-but-good-faith disputes are addressed through a written process before escalation.
The policy lives at a stable URL on the project website. It exists primarily for the moment a hostile fork appears and the maintainers need a document to point at — a moment that arrives faster than most projects expect, and is much harder to handle without a written stance in hand.

# 10. Risk Register

This register lists the risks most likely to threaten the MVP specifically — risks to delivery, rather than the long-term architectural risks catalogued in the blueprint. Each is rated for likelihood and impact, paired with a mitigation, and assigned an owner. The register is intended to be reviewed at every phase boundary.

| Risk | L / I | Mitigation | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| The collectible-load-context memory model proves unreliable in practice. | Med / High | Front-loaded as the first task in phase 1; a permanent CI leak test thereafter. If it fails, the plan pauses for a design correction. | Compiler eng. |
| Scope creep — cloud, agents, or SSO features pulled into the MVP. | High / High | An explicit, written scope boundary (section 3); the delivery lead empowered to defend it; deferred items visibly parked, not rejected. | Delivery lead |
| .NET 8 LTS / Aspire / language-server previews introduce breaking changes. | Med / Med | Track preview releases actively; isolate each dependency behind a narrow internal interface; budget contingency in phase 4. | Tech lead |
| Embedded C# IntelliSense in YAML is harder than estimated. | Med / Med | Treat as the riskiest tooling task; if it slips, ship schema-only YAML support for v1 and add C# intelligence in a fast follow. | Tooling eng. |
| Too few pilot teams, or pilots that do not exercise the tool seriously. | Med / High | Recruit the cohort during phase 3, before the tool is ready; over-recruit; define “serious use” in the success criteria up front. | Delivery lead |
| Orchestration flakiness on diverse developer hardware undermines trust. | Med / High | Health gating and generous timeouts from phase 1; test on a range of machines during the pilot; classify environment errors distinctly. | Orchestration eng. |
| Key-person dependency on the compiler workstream. | Med / High | Two engineers on the workstream from the start; the tech lead reviews all compiler changes to spread context. | Tech lead |
| The provider contract proves wrong in shape after several providers are written against it, forcing a costly rework late in delivery. | Med / High | Drafted in phase 1 and exercised by a throwaway reference provider before phase 2; three real Core providers built against it in phase 2 so design problems surface early; a contract freeze gate at the end of phase 3 before the SDK is published. | Tech lead |
| The community pathway fails to materialise after launch — contributors find the SDK opaque, the documentation thin, or the contribution loop slow. | Med / Med | Phase 4 includes a dry-run by an outside contributor against the v1 SDK, treating any friction as a documentation or contract bug; CONTRIBUTING.md, a worked example provider, and an integration test fixture are part of the v1 deliverable rather than post-launch work. | Tech lead |
| The reporting surface is treated as a hardening task and ships under-polished, eroding the pilot's trust in the tool. | Med / High | Reporting is broken out as its own workstream (G) rather than a Phase 4 bullet; the minimal terminal renderer is the compiler workstream's own integration-test surface from Phase 2, so the event stream and renderer are exercised continuously rather than retro-fitted; the polling timeline and captured-variable thread land in Phase 3 before pilot. | Tech lead |
| Without a sanctioned seeding mechanism, pilot teams improvise brittle data setup and blame the platform. | Low / Med | The declarative seed block is in scope and lands in Phase 2 alongside the first real tests; a recipes guide documents the factory and snapshot alternatives; a failed seed is an environment error, never a misattributed test failure. | Orchestration eng. |
| Secrets are hard-coded into test files, producing a leak and a failed security review. | Med / High | The ${secret:…} syntax with environment-variable and Vault sources is in scope for v1, not deferred; report redaction limits blast radius; a secret-shaped-literal lint rule is a fast follow. | Compiler eng. |
| The runner does not scale to a real test estate — no selection, unsafe parallelism — so teams route around it. | Med / Med | Selection language and scenario-level parallelism with an explicit isolation contract land in Phase 3; the conservative isolation default (private topology per parallel scenario) prevents shared-state flakiness from the start. | Tooling eng. |
| Pilot teams cannot see a path from their existing tests and disengage. | Med / Med | Migration is named as a Phase 5 activity; worked porting examples from Postman, xUnit, and SpecFlow are authored during the pilot; the honest 're-author, not auto-convert' message is set in the first conversation. | Delivery lead |
| The launch lands quietly because no DevRel capacity exists. | Med / High | The tech lead and platform/community engineer jointly own the first thirty days post-launch with explicit response-time commitments (section 9.4); a second post-launch blog post is scheduled at day fourteen; if community pathway viability falls behind by month three, a dedicated DevRel hire is added per section 5.4. | Tech lead |
| Opt-in telemetry produces too little signal to evaluate the success criteria. | Med / Med | Pilots are explicitly asked to opt in as part of the pilot contract (section 8.5); the weekly working sessions and structured retrospectives are the primary evidence stream, with telemetry as confirmation rather than substitute. | Delivery lead |
| The product name is chosen too late and v1.0 ships under the working title. | Low / Med | Naming is a Phase 3 deliverable so that the docs URL, the GitHub organisation, and the launch artifacts can be produced under the chosen name (section 2.6). | Delivery lead |
| The pricing band is wrong by an order of magnitude and the demand-signal evidence is therefore mis-calibrated. | Low / High | The price band is stated as a range, not a number (section 4.4); pilot conversations refine the band before the demand-signal commitment is requested; benchmarks against comparable products are explicit so the hypothesis can be checked. | Delivery lead |
| Accessibility or licence compliance issues surface at launch and damage the platform's credibility. | Low / High | WCAG 2.1 AA is a v1.0 commitment with a Phase 4 accessibility review; the Apache 2.0 licence is paired with DCO contribution and trademark filing (section 9.6); SBOMs and signed binaries are part of the release manifest. | Tech lead |
| The engine breaks the provider contract on a routine release, breaking every community provider in the wild. | Med / High | The v1 provider contract is frozen for the v1.x engine series, with new optional capabilities added via extension interfaces (IStepProviderV1_1) rather than by modifying existing ones; breaking changes appear only in a v2.x engine series with an explicit migration story (architecture blueprint section 13.8.1). The contract-freeze gate at the end of Phase 3 is reviewed against this commitment before the Provider SDK is published. | Tech lead |
| Container image pulls on fresh CI runners exceed the 90-second startup criterion and the pilot reports flaky timeouts. | Med / Med | The 90-second criterion is measured on warmed laptops with cached images; CI templates (Phase 4) include a docker-pull pre-warming step before the test step; documentation recommends self-hosted runners that persist their image cache between jobs and image digest pinning for byte-stable pulls; image-pull failures are classified as environment errors with the registry hostname and auth status named in the report. | Orchestration eng. |
| Enterprise procurement teams cannot adopt the platform because no vendor entity is named. | Med / High | A corporate entity is incorporated in Phase 3 with the product name as trading identity (section 1.2); the entity is the vendor of record on procurement paperwork even for the free Indie tier; legal advice in Phase 3 confirms the jurisdiction and structure before incorporation. | Delivery lead |
| Cloud-tier data-residency commitments are made too late and lose regulated-industry pilots. | Med / High | EU/UK region hosting is committed at v1.0 of the cloud tier as part of the Enterprise tier (section 4.4); the launch communications name the regions and the data-flow boundary explicitly so regulated pilots can pre-screen before investing time. | Tech lead |
| Realistic enterprise adoption skips the Team tier entirely (SSO is non-negotiable), making the Team tier under-monetised relative to its development cost. | Med / Med | The pricing hypothesis explicitly names the Indie-to-Enterprise tier-skip pattern (section 4.4); pilot conversations test which tier customers actually slot into; the Team tier's design absorbs this by emphasising CI-consumption rather than seat-based value for organisations whose engineers are not heavy individual users. | Delivery lead |
| The official CI templates become a supply-chain attack surface for every adopter. | Low / High | The CI-templates repository ships with CODEOWNERS, signed releases, commit-SHA pinning in adoption documentation rather than tag pinning (per industry lessons), and a published security-disclosure process. The templates are reviewed at the same bar as Core providers. | Platform / community eng. |
| A hostile fork uses the project name before the trademark is granted and the maintainers have no written stance. | Low / Med | A drafted trademark policy is published on the website at v1.0 launch (section 9.9), not after the first dispute; the policy is the document the maintainers point at, separately from the filing itself, which can take 12-18 months to grant. | Delivery lead |
| Secret values leak into reports despite the renderer-level redaction because base64, HMAC-signed, or partially-logged forms escape string-match redaction. | Med / High | Architecture blueprint section 17.1.1 specifies a typed SecretString return from Vars.Secrets.Resolve that the renderer explicitly knows never to log, replacing the earlier string-match-based redaction; the security review in Phase 4 includes an explicit penetration of the redaction path on realistic OAuth and AWS-signing scenarios. | Compiler eng. |

*Table 10.1 — MVP risk register (L = likelihood, I = impact).*

# 11. Dependencies, Assumptions, and the Go/No-Go Decision

## 11.1 External dependencies

The MVP depends on a small number of things outside the team's direct control. Each is named here so that it can be tracked rather than assumed.

- **.NET 8 LTS and .NET Aspire. **The MVP is built on these and assumes they remain available and reasonably stable through the delivery window; preview-channel changes are tracked actively.
- **The .NET language server. **Embedded C# IntelliSense reuses existing .NET language tooling rather than reimplementing it; the MVP depends on that tooling being integrable into a VSCode extension.
- **Docker on developer machines. **The local topology requires a working Docker installation on each pilot developer's machine.
- **Pilot teams. **The evidence the MVP produces depends on recruiting willing pilot teams; this is treated as a phase-3 activity, not a phase-5 afterthought.

## 11.2 Key assumptions

The plan rests on several assumptions. If any proves false, the plan should be revisited rather than pushed through. The team is dedicated and not subject to competing demands; the seven-person shape holds for the full window; the underlying libraries do not undergo a disruptive breaking change late in delivery; and the local topology is genuinely sufficient to test the core hypothesis — that is, that teams can form a real opinion about the tool without first experiencing cloud execution.

## 11.3 The go/no-go decision

The MVP is not an end in itself; it is the instrument that informs the largest investment decision the platform faces — whether to build the cloud execution fabric. At the end of phase 5 the project reaches an explicit decision point, evaluated against the gate criteria defined in section 4.2 (Sustained pilot adoption, Behavioural demand signal, Community pathway viability) and read against the post-MVP roadmaps below.

| Decision | Operationalised condition | Consequence and next investment |
|---|---|---|
| **Go — fund the cloud tier** | All three gates met: at least six teams sustained-active for six weeks; at least four signed pre-commitments with at least two paid deposits at the stated price band; at least one external Verified-tier provider merged. Guardrails substantially met. | Begin the Testcontainer Cloud workstream (remote Docker proxying, SSH tunnelling, SaaS backend) as the immediate next investment. The architecture's full vision — cloud fabric in tier two, agentic automation in tier three, performance LAB in tier four, enterprise SSO in tier five — becomes the eighteen-month roadmap, sequenced by the architecture document. |
| **Iterate-locally — deepen the Indie tier** | Adoption gate met; demand-signal gate weak (some interest but few deposits) or community gate weak (engagement but no merged Verified-tier provider yet). At least one guardrail unmet. | A further eight-to-twelve-week cycle on the local product before any cloud spend. Priorities, in order: close the guardrail gap, ship the Wave-2 providers most frequently requested by pilots (typically db-assert.sqlserver and mq-publish.rabbitmq), invest in the developer-experience polish that pilot retrospectives surface, re-test the demand signal at the end of the cycle. Hire a dedicated DevRel role if the community gate is the weakness. |
| **Pivot — reshape around what worked** | Pilot teams value some aspect of the tool strongly but not the central hypothesis. For example: they love the Provider SDK as a community framework but use the engine little, or they want the reporting layer as a standalone library. | Reshape the project around the value that landed. The Provider SDK can become a standalone open-source project; the reporting library can become a separate offering. The cloud-tier investment is paused, and the team and budget are reallocated to the surface that earned demand. |
| **Stop — reassess the premise** | Adoption gate not met (fewer than four teams sustained-active for six weeks) or pilots explicitly conclude the declarative approach is not meaningfully better than their existing tools. | Pause major investment. Document the learnings, open-source what has been built, and revisit the strategy with the executive sponsor before more is spent. This is a real outcome that the plan does not pretend is impossible. |

*Table 11.1 — The structured decision the MVP exists to inform. The four-outcome model replaces the simpler three-outcome version that earlier drafts of this plan used, because pilot reality rarely produces a clean binary and the team must know what to do with ambiguous evidence before encountering it.*

Two design points are worth recording about this decision. First, the gates are conjunctive: all three must be met for an unambiguous Go. A project that hits adoption and demand strongly but produces zero external community providers has validated the testing-tool hypothesis but not the open-source strategy that the architecture builds on; that gap is information, not a footnote. Second, the Iterate-locally outcome is not a delay; it is a deliberate further investment with its own time-box and its own re-test point, because perpetual iteration on a weak signal consumes the budget more slowly but no less completely than the wrong Go. Framing the decision this explicitly is the point of the entire plan. By deferring the cloud, the agents, the lab, and enterprise SSO, the MVP keeps the project's largest costs unspent until the project's most important question has been answered with real evidence rather than optimism.

# 12. Plan Summary

The MVP described in this plan is a deliberately narrow slice of a broad vision. It is a locally executing integration-testing tool: a developer installs it, writes tests in the YAML DSL with full editor support, and runs them against a microservice topology provisioned on their own machine. It excludes the cloud fabric, the agentic automation, the performance lab, and the enterprise tier — not because those lack value, but because none of them is needed to answer the one question that determines whether the rest is worth building.

The plan sequences roughly twenty-four weeks of work for a seven-person team across five risk-ordered phases, front-loading the hardest unknowns — memory-safe dynamic compilation and reliable orchestration — into the first phase so that a fundamental problem would be found early and cheaply. It names the user the platform is for and the alternatives it competes against rather than treating those as self-evident. It defines quantified, categorised success criteria — separating gates from guardrails — and a working price hypothesis the pilot programme tests. It designs the pilot programme as a real product activity rather than a coordination task, with recruitment beginning in Phase 3 and a six-week working window in Phase 5. It specifies the launch and the first thirty days post-launch as deliberate work rather than a release event, and it ends at a four-outcome go/no-go decision in which the evidence gathered from real pilot teams, not internal conviction, determines whether the platform proceeds to its cloud tier.

> **The plan in one sentence**
>
> Build the smallest version that lets real .NET teams genuinely experience declarative, orchestrated integration testing on their own machines, put it into their hands through a deliberately designed pilot and launch, and let their behaviour — measured against gates fixed in advance — decide what gets built next.

— End of the MVP Project Plan. The companion documents are the Technical Architecture & Engineering Blueprint and the YAML DSL Specification & VSCode Extension Design.
